If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed.......and we will deserve it.

The wheels of history grind slowly, but they do grind. By the time of his death, Graham was amongst the lickspittlest of Trump’s GOP toadies. Graham’s idiot sister ran for his vacant Senate seat in South Carolina and lost.

Former representative Liz Cheney, at the January 6 hearings in 2021:

I say this to my Republican colleagues who are defending the indefensible. There will come a day when Donald Trump is gone, but your dishonor will remain.

Winston Churchill, perhaps apocryphally:

Americans can always be trusted to do the right thing, once all other possibilities have been exhausted.

Abraham Lincoln:

You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time, but you can not fool all of the people all of the time.

 ★

title: Goodhart's Law, but We Already Spent All Our Money
content:
Here is how to make any sports fan angry. Basketball is just a bunch of grown men bouncing a ball and throwing it into a basket. Football is a bunch of grown men running on grass trying to kick a ball into a net, yes that football. And baseball... Oh boy, baseball.

I've used these lines many times to piss people off and to justify my complete lack of athletic feats. But the counter-argument I always get is that football is a multi-billion-dollar industry, or that a specific player makes more money than I will ever see in a lifetime. If I counter that video games are just for kids, because of course I'd say that, I get a similar response: Video games make more money than all of these sports combined.

It's all true. But nobody is telling me why basketball is important. Nobody tells me how good the game is, how people bond over it, how it brings a community together, or that it is simply healthy to stay active. Whether it's basketball, football, video games, or (God forgive me) baseball, it all boils down to the exact same measuring stick: how much money the activity generates.

If the importance of a thing is only measured by how much money it makes, then we will aim to make more money despite the thing itself. — An AI Somewhere.

Goodhart's Law states that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Enter Artificial Intelligence.

This wave of generative AI has supposedly generated billions of dollars since ChatGPT first launched. But in the process, vastly more money was spent to make it possible. Money was spent to make AI look good. AI is deemed "good" because it is expected to make lots of money. Because AI isn't actually making that money back yet, it relies on inflated valuations to define its worth in monetary terms.

It's like running a pizzeria where the goal is to make a million pizzas, but you don't actually have the ingredients to bake them. Instead of buying flour and tomatoes, you use AI to generate high-resolution photos of delicious pizzas and print them on empty boxes where the future pizza will be. You sell the hype of the box, promising that the actual pizza will arrive once the funding hits.

There is this simple argument, almost naive I would say: If AI is going to take all our jobs, who is going to pay for it?

If workers are displaced, they have no income. If they have no income, they have no purchasing power. Who is this mythical customer who doesn't work, receives no paycheck, yet seamlessly pays a monthly subscription for enterprise AI tools?

Currently, the primary consumer of AI isn't the public buying a finished product. Instead, it's corporations selling AI back and forth to each other in an enterprise circular economy, funded by venture capital that expects infinite returns on a product nobody has fully figured out how to monetize at scale.

This may be an anecdote where N = {"my coworkers over the past four years"}, but in that short timespan, we were visited by the Four Horsemen of Corporate AI.

The First Horseman told us never to touch AI, warning of IP theft and security leaks. The Second Horseman told us to use it cautiously "where needed." The Third Horseman turned AI into a game, tracking metrics to see who could use it the most, (the winner got a free iphone). The Fourth Horseman arrived recently, asking us to stop using Fable, and get written managerial approval to exceed a reduced token budget.

Each horseman was a paid consultant hired to provide training. In just a few years, corporate sentiment swung from paranoia to forced obsession, and finally to budget panic. Employees went from being pushed to "Tokenmaxx" everything to being scolded that tokens cost real money.

AI is important because we spend so much money on it.

When an industry measures success by the dollar amount poured into it rather than the actual utility derived from it, we start living in a fantasy. We spent astronomical sums of money to build AI because we believed it was valuable. Now, we must prove it is valuable simply because we spent all that money.

If we keep measuring the value of technology solely by market capitalizations and speculative hype rather than usefulness, we shouldn't be surprised when people stop buying empty pizza boxes. Beautifully printed empty pizza boxes I should say. Right now, we are running out of money to buy the ingredients to actually make the pizza.

The AI fatfinger economy has come for my receipts app (permalink)

"AI is being shoved down our throats" can mean any of several things. It can mean that our bosses are demanding that we use AI in reckless or nonsensical ways on the job:

https://www.404media.co/manifestos-fear-and-loser-thinking-inside-protons-ai-reckoning/

It can mean that Elon Musk and the NASDAQ have colluded to force ordinary retirement savers to bail out his emirati and tech oligarch buddies:

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/05/technology/spacex-indexes-401k.html

These are arguably the most important ways in which AI is shoved down our throats, but the most visible form of conscription into the number-go-up AI project is happening at the user interface level. This UI fuckery predates AI. For more than a decade, tech companies and their executives have colluded to trick, coerce and force you into using new features that they wanted to sell to their investors as the future of their companies.

Remember Google Plus, the Facebook-killing social layer that was going to give Google access to a new, multi-trillion-dollar market? Bradley Horowitz, then a VP at Google, charged every product team with cramming G+ into their offerings, tying their bonuses to G+ usage (at companies like Google, your bonus can dwarf your base salary).

Now, googlers are bright and resourceful people, and if you tell them that they can double their earnings by getting users to click on Google Plus buttons, they'll come up with all kinds of ways to get you to do this. Some of those gambits will be the kind of thing that Horowitz doubtless hoped for: innovative and creative ways to add value to Google's core offerings with G+ features.

But when the stakes are that high, Goodhart's Law inevitably comes into play: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure":

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law

The easiest way to get a user to click on a G+ button is to replace whatever button that user hits most often with a G+ version. Rather than introducing users to Google Plus in a way that turns them into G+ fans, you just frustrate them by tricking them into clicking on a useless button.

From a product manager's perspective, it's worth making whatever changes as are needed to ensure that your salary is doubled because you hit your "key performance indicator" (KPI), even if it's at the expense of your users' loyalty to your product. Preserving user loyalty at the expense of half your wages is a bad trade.

When a machine learning system does this, we call it "reward hacking." AI programmers create an "objective function" for their system, a single number that the system will try every tactic to increase; then, more often than not, the AI program finds perverse shortcuts to make the number go up whether or not it achieves the programmer's goal:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reward_hacking

For example, if you charge an AI with coming up with the shortest run through a video game, it might well discover a bug that makes it impervious to enemy attacks or just lets it teleport to the end of the game. To avoid these perverse outcomes, programmers have to add more and more specificity to their objective functions: "speed run the game without teleporting or discovering an immortality hack."

Not for nothing, many science fiction writers (including me) have noted that tech bosses' fear of their own AI systems is a kind of emotional spillover from their frustrations with the corporations they run, where underlings engage in the same kinds of reward hacking that we see from chatbots:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/04/14/timmy-share/#a-superior-moral-justification-for-selfishness

Despite the ease with which metrics can be gamed, tech bosses remained committed to the use of KPIs to shift the priorities of their organizations, and they use the same objective function refinement technique that programmers use for reward-hacking AIs in a bid to prevent cheating by employees who hit their KPIs any way they can.

This explains a lot about the experience of watching a video on your phone. Any time you tune into a show on a streaming platform, you are forced to handle your phone with the delicacy of a photonegative. If any part of your hand brushes any part of the screen, you will immediately be whisked away from the video you're watching to an entirely different one:

https://pluralistic.net/2022/05/15/the-fatfinger-economy/

Worse, after your program has been replaced with this new one, there's no obvious way to get back to the show you were just watching. This is very weird, considering that the "back button" has been a part of computer interfaces since 1981:

https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/back%20button

The reason you don't get a back button is reward hacking. Streaming video platforms are under enormous pressure to successfully recommend their back-catalog to their users, because the alternative (commissioning or purchasing a steady stream of popular new shows) is very expensive. Investors put a lot of stock in streaming services' "successful recommendation" rate.

So streaming service bosses charge their product teams with making "successful recommendations." The easiest way to "recommend a show" is to booby-trap the streaming service's UI so that touching any part of the screen takes you to a video you never asked to see.

This is obvious reward hacking, so streaming bosses refined their objective function: they made their teams' bonuses contingent on getting you to watch a new video for a minimum time-frame. This in turn triggered the next volley in the reward-hacking wars, in which product teams took away the back button. This gives users any number of greased slides that whisk them away to a new video. To get back to the old video, users are forced to climb a greased pole.

This is the fatfinger economy: created in the 2010s by teams at large tech companies with KPI-obsessed bosses; refined in the 2020s by teams at bottom-line obsessed streaming media companies; and now perfected by teams being charged with cramming AI into every corner of our lives:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/05/02/kpis-off/#principal-agentic-ai-problem

The fatfinger economy is an extraordinary beneficiary of the drive to add "telemetry" to all of our apps. Today, an app vendor can call up a dashboard and find out which buttons and fields and sliders see the most use, and they can use that ranked list to figure out which buttons to replace with AI-demon-summoning lookalikes that help product teams "prove" to their bosses that they've "successfully integrated AI" and lets their bosses prove to their investors that "users value AI features."

I recently switched from Android to Graphene, a de-googled phone operating system. Graphene's maintainers are blissfully free from the imperative to show that "users value AI features," and that's why I have never accidentally summoned up an undismissable AI by tapping a Graphene UI element.

It's a different story when it comes to apps. Graphene has many different ways to install apps, including via Google Play (Google's default Android store). That's useful because it lets you install your old Android apps after switching to Graphene, but it does leave you exposed to the fatfinger economy.

Last week, I got a painful reminder of the progress of the fatfinger economy outside of Graphene's utopian pocket-universe. I make extensive use of an app called "Genius Scanner," which lets me scan receipts and email them to myself (I do this a lot because, as a freelancer, I have to track a lot of different expenses). I bought a lifetime subscription to Genius Scanner in 2023, after getting burned by Camscanner (my previous, now enshittified scanning app), and I've been perfectly happy with it…until now.

Genius Scanner is obviously under pressure to drive AI adoption. I can tell because they've taken away the most important UI element and swapped it for a worse-than-useless AI button.

Here's how I use Genius Scanner: I press the "make new scan" button and line up the receipt on the screen. Then I press the "retitle" button, which brings up a field that is populated with the current date and time (16 characters in all). This text used to be selected so that hitting the little "x" next to it deleted it, making it easy to title a new scan. After that, I'd just email it to myself.

As of last week, though, there is no button that deletes the date and time so you can enter a useful title. That little "x" has been replaced with a button that brings up an ad for the company's new AI tools, which cost $40/year. There's no way to tell the system that you're not interested in buying a new subscription for the tool that you've already bought a lifetime sub for, and there's no way to get that little "x" back.

To be clear: that little "x" represents one quarter of my receipt scanning workflow. They have swapped it out for an ad for a new subscription AI feature, and gave me 16 new keypresses on the backspace button to replace that single tap on the "x." I have seen that ad about 100 times at this point, because I keep tapping the spot where the "x" used to be.

I'm certain that the company knew that its paying customers relied on the "x" to accomplish a vital function in any scanning app (giving good, descriptive titles to scans). They need the AI number to go up, so they replaced the "x" with the AI ad, which will let them tell their investors that they've got "strong consumer interest in their AI features."

Meanwhile, they already have my money, so there's no way I can punish them for their decision to screw me over to juke a meaningless stat. It's as neat (and depressing) an example of the principle that "even if you're paying for the product, you're still the product" that you could ask for.

It's also a perfect little object-lesson in the ways that companies can report increasing AI interest and usage without generating any interest or usage. In the fatfinger economy, every metric is a target, and is thereby rendered meaningless.

title: Book Review: Practice by Rosalind Brown ★★★★☆
content:
I have a simple rule - if I meet someone at a party and they say they've written a book, then I will immediately buy that book. It's a strategy which has worked out well; leading me to some truly interesting and delightful prose.

Rosalind Brown (a fellow UEA graduate) has written a stunning little book. Practice is an almost Proustian meander through a day-in-the-life of a young woman going through an essay crisis. Much like R. F. Kuang's "Katabasis", I'm rather glad the author found university to be a bewildering and, at times, upsetting experience as it provides rich fodder for this tale.

There is an inherent tragedy in studying English literature. The more you read, the more futile it becomes. Just like repeatedly saying a word aloud creates semantic satiation, so to does the repeated reading of sonnets drive away all their meaning. The closer you study a poem the further it slips from your grasp. The more introspective you become, the more you lose sight of what you really want out of life.

As Proverbs 26:11 suggests, some students are like a snake which is compelled to eat its own tail. The protagonist, Annabel, isn't a caricature but she sure is a trope that you've met in halls. She's a woe-is-me wretch who'd rather cultivate a "Heated Rivalry" style interior monologue rather than engage with those around her. So self-absorbed to that she doesn't realise that, not only do other people have feelings, other people are carrying the same burden she does. I suspect her essay research really should have widened to include the seminal "Male gays in the female gaze"!

It's a short novel, but pleasingly thorough. Although there aren't any major twists, I can't say I predicted how the story would evolve and conclude. The punctuation and sentence structure is charmingly idiosyncratic and, I think, perfectly fits the story.

A note on formatting. The ePub has hard page breaks. That means some "pages" contain little more than a paragraph. I suspect that's intentional as it gives a wonderfully staccato pace to the text. Our day is broken up into little moments which don't quite fit the strictures of a chapter, yet we experience the day as a cohesive whole.

An excellent book - but one to read after you've finished your homework.

title: This Week in Source Control: 4 November 2026
content:
This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.

Scaling

Scaling Git at OpenAI (Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau and Ted Nyman, OpenAI) describes Pando, a Rust backend for git repositories that now serves all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Each push is stored as an immutable packfile in blob storage, and each branch update records a ref version in a metadata store, so pushes contend only when they target the same ref. The trade-off is causal consistency, so a client reading several branches can see them at different points in time.

When a new branch is pushed, Pando advertises only trunk, which keeps the pushed pack reusable for anyone who already has trunk, and the median pack produced this way was under 20 KiB. On a fetch, Pando sends an empty packfile in the response and lists the packs the client needs as packfile-uri links. The client downloads those packs from a regional cache with a hit rate above 99%.

Background compaction merges small packs into larger ones in levels, up to L4 in the monorepo, and the levels double as a skip list for choosing which packs a client needs. OpenAI reports median push latency down by nearly 80% and nearly a petabyte of git data served a day. Fixes to packfile-uri downloads have gone upstream, and other changes, such as downloading and indexing packs in parallel, are in OpenAI’s git fork.

An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke (typesanitizer) responds to Anthropic’s Scion post from someone on the source control team at Databricks, whose monorepo’s main branch history is 20-50GB. The author lists the parts of Scion’s design that already exist in Mononoke, Perforce or Piper, such as per-directory ACLs, server-side history queries and changesets in place of git trees.

They also question Anthropic’s mirror count: Databricks serves CI from fewer than 10 git mirrors and reference repositories refreshed every two hours, while Anthropic reported running several hundred mirrors at its peak.

Building fine-grained version control for agents (Antonio Scandurra, Delta) describes DeltaDB from the team behind Zed. Each agent thread is a DAG of CRDT deltas stored in SQLite on the client and synced to one Cloudflare Durable Object per thread.

Worktrees are layered on top of git, starting from a commit and recording edits as deltas, and creating a commit adds a delta that links the DAG back to git’s history. Subagents work on separate timelines in the same DAG and merge back into it, and coordinating agents this way needs no git commit.

GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September (Frederic Lardinois, The New Stack) reports figures from GitHub Universe. GitHub had 1.4 billion commits a month in April and 2.9 billion in August. It has added 4 million CPU cores and 160 PB of storage this year, alongside the move to separate compute and storage covered in last week’s issue.

Releases

Sapling 0.2.20261028 makes sl worktree work in checkouts made with git clone, using git worktree add underneath, and ships it in builds without EdenFS, including the open source ones. sl drop -r REV is now on by default and removes commits from a stack, rebasing their descendants.

This release also adds a --plan flag to histedit for giving the plan on the command line, plus an into verb that folds the previous commit in while keeping the current message. Rewriting a commit in the middle of a stack now works with uncommit too. 0.2.20261102 fixes a regression from that release, where files under directories matched by rules like target/ showed up as untracked and nested .gitignore files were skipped.

OmniDiff 0.3.0 is the latest release of Marko Ivankovic’s content-aware difftool in Rust. It was on Hacker News this week and diffs code by syntax, along with pictures, fonts, archives and PDFs. This release diffs code embedded in strings as its own language, for example shell in a YAML run: block or CSS in template literals, and diffs CSS class lists one class at a time.

The GitRoot 0.5.0 plugins include Firefly, which is written in Zig and generates status pages inside the forge. Silo, which builds indexes from files and their metadata, can now render them to the web grouped by any property, and Apex, the plugin that renders repository files to the web, adds a slide layout.

gt 1.0.0 is the first stable release of the Gitea command line tool introduced last week, and it replaces tea as Gitea’s official CLI. tea is discontinued and its repository archived. A migration guide maps its commands and flags to gt’s. Commands, flags, --json fields and exit codes now follow semantic versioning. Changes since 0.1.0 include:

  • gt upgrade replaces the binary after checking its SHA-256 checksum, or names the package manager command when gt came from Homebrew, Nix, a Linux package or go install.
  • Extensions named gt-NAME install from any Gitea instance, and GitHub CLI extensions that avoid GitHub’s APIs also run.
  • gt pr backport cherry-picks a merged pull request onto one or more release branches and opens a pull request into each.
  • Every command with --json also takes --csv.

git-loom 1.0 merges a set of feature branches into one integration branch, where they are built and tested together. Its commands commit, amend, split and move changes between those branches while the integration branch stays checked out, and rewrite history so each stays a side branch joined by a merge.

Stacked branches are pushed as one pull request each to GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps or Gerrit. Commits get short IDs from a Change-Id trailer, so the IDs stay the same across rewrites. With 1.0 the commands, loom.* settings and agent mode follow semantic versioning, and it requires Git 2.43 or later.

difftastic 0.72.0 changes its preprocessing heuristics so it falls back to text diffing less often, and updates the Haskell and Kotlin parsers. Verilog, F# and Smali support is removed. The Verilog and F# parsers made the difft binary large, and the upstream Smali parser is unmaintained. It also fixes terminal width detection when stdin, stdout and stderr are all redirected, which broke in 0.71 and was most noticeable when running difft from jj.

GitButler 0.23.2 stops commits and amends from disturbing staged files, and undo now restores deleted branches after a git garbage collection. Merge request listing also works on older GitLab instances. On the command line, but agent setup adds Amp support, and but worktree new --above takes branch names and IDs as well as git revisions.

Also out: forges v0.3.1.

Security

Gitea 28.3.0 fixes 21 CVEs, many of them places where public-only tokens could reach private data or admin actions. Among them:

  • With ACCOUNT_LINKING = auto and open registration, someone signing in through an OAuth2 provider could enter another user’s name or email and be linked to that existing account with only the OAuth2 sign-in (CVE-2026-120263).
  • A user with read access could submit a pull request review whose commit_id named their own commit, so pull_request_review workflows ran from that commit with the repository’s secrets and a write token (CVE-2026-118386).
  • A site administrator’s public-only token could use the admin API to list every user’s email address and create new administrators (CVE-2026-117635).
  • An organization owner’s public-only token had enough access to delete all of the organization’s repositories, private ones included (CVE-2026-119441).
  • Release binaries are built with Go 1.27.3, which rejects certificates chained through the eMudhra intermediates, for Gitea’s outgoing connections to OAuth2 providers, webhooks, mirrors and migrations (CVE-2026-111943). Saturday’s package management roundup has more on that incident, including a test page showing that the git Apple ships with macOS still accepts those certificates.

Alpine Linux rebuilt its GitLab instance after an attacker tried to exploit CVE-2026-97229 on 20 and 21 October. The bug is in Onigmo, Ruby’s regular expression engine, and GitLab’s fix is a patch applied to the Ruby in its official packages. Alpine’s image used standard Ruby, so upgrading GitLab on 22 October left it vulnerable.

The attacker crashed worker processes eight times, and Alpine found no evidence of code execution. A check on 26 October turned up the unpatched Ruby, and the instance was rebuilt and reopened on 29 October. The aports repository and packages, including the 21 October releases, were checked against outside records, and all passwords were reset. GitLab installs that use their own Ruby also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.

Scanning 7.25M public repositories on Gitee for secrets (Ben Zimmermann, MongoDB) found 26,400 unique verified-live credentials using TruffleHog and Kingfisher. The only official Gitee API endpoint that returned useful data at that size was user search, so the repository list was built from that, Explore feeds, per-user pages and the Elasticsearch widget behind the site’s search. GitHub runs secret-scanning partnerships with credential issuers, and Gitee has no public equivalent.

GitHub

GitHub Desktop 3.6.10 and later can sign in with short-lived tokens that refresh automatically for API requests and git operations. The rollout is gradual and covers github.com only. Existing tokens stay as they are, and an installation gets short-lived tokens at its first sign-in after the rollout reaches it.

The 3.6.8 release notes list the change alongside Git 2.56.0, Git LFS 3.8.1 and Git Credential Manager 2.9.1. 3.6.10 bundles Git for Windows 2.56.0.windows.4, whose brotli upgrade to 1.2.1 fixes CVE-2026-111497.

Pull request limits can now exempt contributors by account age or by number of merged pull requests in that repository. A contributor who meets either enabled rule can open pull requests beyond the cap.

Push protection can block AI-detected secrets, in public preview, using a classifier that scores a value by how the surrounding code uses it, in place of format matching. GitHub reports it more than doubled the number of pushes where push protection caught a secret. It is opt-in and requires AI-detected secret scanning and push protection to be enabled first.

The Meta API now lists three more IP ranges for webhook deliveries in its hooks field. Static allowlists for incoming webhooks need the new CIDR prefixes added.

Elsewhere

Tangled has relaunched as a federated code forge on the AT Protocol. Knot2, a rewrite of its git server in Rust, stores issues, pull requests, comments and labels in the repository as collaborative objects, chains of git objects synced over the AT Protocol firehose. Each edit also writes an attestation record to the author’s own PDS.

The release adds organization accounts and stacked pull requests with interdiffs for git and jj users. A new Svelte frontend is served from read-only Rust indexers in 11 or more regions, and self-hosted knots need upgrading to v1.20.0.

David Bushell responded to the new Tangled UI with an accessibility review. The interface sets text at 12px, and a font-size: 16px on the <html> element fixes the root size regardless of browser settings. Forcing a 200% resize clips and truncates text, which fails WCAG 2.2’s 1.4.4 Resize Text criterion.

Forgejo is removing OpenID 2.0 sign-in in v19, due on 25 March 2027, and keeping OpenID Connect and OAuth. The v15 LTS keeps OpenID 2.0 until its end of life on 15 July 2027, and v17 and v18 keep it until 29 April 2027.

Git Rev News 140 leads with a fix for git push --force-if-includes, which rejected valid force pushes when the remote-tracking ref had no reflog. A ref created by git clone with the files backend gets its first reflog entry when it moves, and before that a cut-off timestamp was left uninitialised.

Aleksei Sviridkin’s one-line patch sets it to 0. In review Junio Hamano suggested a 90-day cut-off, then agreed to 0 after Tyler Cipriani described a case with default gc settings where the cut-off gives the wrong answer.

The first version of the patch carried an Assisted-by: LLM trailer following Linux kernel practice. After Junio pointed to the AI section of Git’s SubmittingPatches, version 3 of the patch dropped the trailer.

Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

title: “It Gives Great Demo”
content:
There’s that famous video of Steve Jobs explaining why they don’t didn’t make touchscreen MacBooks:

We thought about [a touch screen MacBook] years ago. We’ve done tons of user testing on this and it turns out it doesn’t work! Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives great demo. But after a short period of time, you start to fatigue. And after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off. It doesn’t work. It’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal […] that’s why we’ve perfected our multitouch trackpads over the years.

I’m not going to weigh in on the new MacBooks. But what I find specifically intriguing in this video — and broadly relevant — is that phrase: “It gives great demo.”

Damn, that is a great line for so much of technology.

“It gives great demo.”

Something that looks amazing when it’s presented to you, but in practical day-to-day use you discover, “Actually this is kinda terrible.”

Demo is everything nowadays. Whatever can garner attention. Who cares if it works in practice, does it give great demo? Because demo time is sale time.

The purpose of a demo is to get your attention. To make you think about the product and that it exists. But a great product often makes you forget it exists at all.

It seems like a paradox: we’re attracted to what stands out, but we become enamored with what disappears.

Of course, this doesn’t just apply to products. People can give great demo, too. You can make a whole career out of just giving great demo.
